reason: The sources provide 20 robust, multi-sourced claims that easily support a highly surprising 45-second story about fast radio bursts.
story: In 2007, astronomers searching through archival data from Australia's Parkes Observatory discovered a mind-bending cosmic mystery: the first Fast Radio Burst (FRB). These millisecond-long flashes of deep-space radio waves are incredibly powerful, discharging as much energy in a fraction of a second as our Sun does in days. Yet, because they travel across billions of light-years, their signals are incredibly weak by the time they reach Earth—one thousand times fainter than a cell phone signal on the Moon! Scientists estimate that up to ten thousand of these bursts happen across the sky every single day. While they were long thought to be one-off, cataclysmic destructions, the discovery of repeating burst FRB 121102 shattered that theory. Even more shocking, researchers recently found 'ultra-fast' radio bursts from this same source that last a mere ten millionths of a second, revealing a hidden, hyper-rapid universe.
angle: Fast radio bursts release as much energy in a millisecond as the Sun does in days, but reach Earth 1,000 times fainter than a cell phone signal on the Moon.

claims.claim: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) were first discovered in 2007.
The first FRB was discovered by astrophysicist Duncan Lorimer.
FRBs typically last only a few milliseconds.
A single FRB can release more energy in a millisecond than the Sun does in an entire day or several days.
By the time an FRB signal reaches Earth, it is extremely weak, about 1,000 times fainter than a cell phone signal broadcasting from the Moon.
Most FRBs are extragalactic, meaning they originate far outside our Milky Way galaxy.
Scientists estimate that up to 10,000 fast radio bursts occur across the sky every single day.
The very first FRB was found in archival data recorded by the Parkes Observatory in Australia.
The data containing the first FRB was recorded in the year 2001.
FRB 121102 was the first repeating fast radio burst source ever discovered.
FRB 121102 is located in a dwarf galaxy approximately 3 billion light-years away from Earth.
The radio waves from FRB 121102 are highly polarized.
FRB 121102's bursts undergo extreme Faraday rotation, which is the twisting of radio waves as they pass through magnetized plasma.
The Faraday rotation of FRB 121102's bursts is about 500 times higher than that of any other FRB detected up to that time.
Magnetars, which are highly magnetic neutron stars, are a leading hypothesized source of FRBs.
In 2020, astronomers detected the first FRB originating inside our own Milky Way galaxy and linked it to a magnetar.
Astronomers have discovered ultra-fast radio bursts that last only millionths of a second (microseconds) or less.
These ultra-fast, microsecond-duration bursts were detected from the repeating source FRB 121102.
FRB 110523 was detected by the Green Bank Telescope in West Virginia.
FRB 110523 was recorded in the year 2011.

disputed: The exact recording date of the first FRB: S1 states it occurred on July 24, 2001, whereas S4 states it occurred on August 24, 2001. A script should state the year (2001) without specifying the month to avoid this conflict.

The duration of the first FRB: S1 states it was less than 5 milliseconds in duration, while S4 describes it as a five-millisecond burst. A script should generalize it as lasting approximately five milliseconds.

Whether FRB 121102 was the only repeating source at the time: S5 states it is the only known repeating source, whereas S1 and S6 note that many other repeating FRBs have since been found. A script should clarify that it was the first repeating source discovered, not the only one.
